title: Knowledge Check 11: Lessons 81-87
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 81-87 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A board deck states: "95 percent of AI pilots fail, only 39 percent of companies see EBIT impact, so fewer than half of programs pay back." The lesson objects to this sentence on what grounds?
options: The 95 percent figure comes from vendors rather than independent research, so it should be discarded entirely
The three figures are stale, because AI spending rose 49.5 percent, which invalidates earlier survey data

The figures measure different things: 95 percent is the share of analyzed deployments with no measurable P&L impact, 39 percent is the share of survey respondents attributing any enterprise EBIT impact, and they do not share a denominator
The 39 percent figure already includes the 95 percent failure rate, so citing both double-counts the same organizations
questions.explanation: The lesson walks through each source and then names the temptation to stack them into one arc, calling that a well-formatted composite no source supports. It also notes the 77 percent board figure has no performance content at all.

questions.question: In the invoice exception worked example, the case stays net positive even when the auto-clear rate falls to 10 percent. What does the lesson say explains that?
options: The remaining human reviews are cheaper because the agent prepared the evidence packet, so the workflow saves time even when the agent's proposal is not used automatically
Inference costs are so low that they are immaterial at any acceptance rate, so the benefit side carries the case alone
The baseline of 22 minutes per exception was overstated, so a lower auto-clear rate still beats it
Sample review of auto-cleared cases drops to zero as the rate falls, which releases enough hours to offset the slower tail
questions.explanation: The lesson states the value comes less from autonomy than from packet preparation that shortens every remaining human decision, and that the agent does not have to be right to be useful, only fast at making the next human decision faster.

questions.question: A team presents the invoice case with the same model and the same 40 percent auto-clear rate, but they removed the validator gate so analysts review every agent proposal from scratch. What does the lesson predict?
options: Payback stretches to about 9 months, because inference cost roughly doubles without caching
The case improves, because analysts keep full control and spend less time on policy exceptions
Hours freed falls to zero and the system costs about $13,053 a month while saving nothing, which is the shape of most failed pilots
The NPV stays near $1 million, because the build cost is already sunk by the time the gate is removed
questions.explanation: The lesson describes this exact variant: without the gate the analyst redoes the full 22 minutes to check the draft, hours freed drops to zero, and the cost stack of roughly $13,053 a month buys no savings. It also adds the error line that can make even the best sensitivity case a loss.

questions.question: A program has spent 180,000 dollars on the agent build and the ERP integration, 3,000 dollars a month on run and eval upkeep, and has no budget line for process redesign or capability building. Per the lesson, what does this spend shape indicate?
options: The program is in good shape, because the payback math from the invoice queue case does not depend on training spend
The build line is underweighted, so the auto-clear rate will stay below the 40 percent design assumption
The program is buying a capability it has not decided how to absorb, because capability building was treated as an implementation detail while technology took the money and attention
The ratio is correct, since the one to three to five pattern applies only to programs with a budget above one million dollars
questions.explanation: The lesson states the 1:3:5 finding as a diagnostic rather than a budget rule: if technology is the largest of the three numbers, the program is buying a capability it has not decided how to absorb, and it applies that reading directly to the 180,000 dollar build with no line for redesign or capability building.

questions.question: The AP lead reports that all six analysts finished the two-hour training session and asks whether the team is ready for go-live. According to the lesson, what is still missing?
options: A completion dashboard with per-analyst timestamps, so the sponsor can see the training landed

A proficiency gate: twenty real cases including the ugly ones, decisions scored by a reviewer against a stated threshold, a written note on deliberate departures, and a dated retry path for anyone who fails
A follow-up class scheduled thirty days after go-live to refresh the material once people have used the tool
Nothing, because finishing the session closes the knowledge stage and the ability stage follows automatically with practice
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the gap sits between knowledge and ability, that training completion indicates information was received rather than that it can be applied under real conditions, and it lists the four parts of a working gate: real evidence set, scored dry run, stated threshold, retry path with a date.

questions.question: A team has run the weekly triage for eight weeks and produced meeting notes every time, with no eval cases, no policy changes and no tool fixes. Per the lesson, what is happening and what is the fix?
options: The agent is performing well enough that no changes are needed, so the meetings should continue as passive monitoring
The intake schema needs more free-text fields, so analysts can describe problems in richer detail
The loop is capturing without closing, and the fix is to promote at least one corrected answer into the offline eval set each week and require it to be named in the notes
Triage should move to a monthly cadence so each item has time to mature before a decision is made
questions.explanation: The lesson treats the output of a feedback loop as a change to the system, calls a loop with zero conversions for two weeks decorative, and prescribes exactly that fix: promote at least one corrected answer into the offline eval set and name it, since the corrected answer is the field that becomes a test case.

questions.question: An engineer opens the architecture review for the invoice exception queue by running a live demo on ten invoices, all of which the agent handles correctly, and offers it as the evidence that the design is sound. Per the lesson, why does the room discount this?
options: Because demos are not permitted in a design review, since the packet is the only accepted artifact
Because ten invoices is too small a sample for a rate calculation, so the demo should have used the full three thousand exceptions
Because a demo proves a path exists on one day, and stochastic behavior means it does not prove the path is the normal path, so the review needs eval numbers plus one honest failing case
Because the agent's stochastic output means the demo cannot be reproduced, which makes it inadmissible as an engineering claim
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the demo as the argument and "it works" as evidence among the traps. With stochastic behavior, a demo shows that a path exists, not that it is the normal path, and reviewers who have seen an agent fail after a good demo discount it. The prescribed replacement is the evidence page with a pass rate, a sample size, a named held-out set, and one failing case, because the failing case is what makes the numbers believable.

questions.question: During the review, an engineer from another team argues that the queue should have been built on a different agent framework, and the framework sits behind a clean boundary with a low reversal cost. Per the lesson, what is the correct handling?
options: Concede it in the first five minutes and spend the room's attention on the high-reversal decisions, because a reversible choice is not worth debate
Defend the framework choice, because conceding anything early signals that the design is weak and invites further challenges
Add the framework debate to the parking list and schedule a separate review to decide it before the pilot starts
Escalate the disagreement to the decision owner, because two engineers disagreeing requires a formal resolution path
questions.explanation: The tradeoff table's reversal-cost column is described as the argument-settling column: low-reversal decisions are conceded early and visibly, which buys credibility for the argument about the expensive ones. The lesson names the framework choice when the boundary is clean as a first-five-minutes concession, alongside prompt wording, module boundaries, naming and dashboard layout.

questions.question: The decision owner closes the invoice queue review with a conditional approval, and one of the conditions has no named owner and no date. Per the lesson, how should the team read that outcome?
options: As an approval, since conditional approval is the normal outcome and owners can be assigned later during delivery planning
As a deferral of the whole design until the evidence page carries a complete set of measured numbers
As a rejection in disguise, because a condition with no owner and no date cannot be enforced and will quietly not be met
As a signal that the decision owner wants the low-confidence record replaced before the pilot starts
questions.explanation: The lesson states that the normal outcome is approved with conditions, and that every condition must have an owner and a date, because a condition without a date is a rejection in disguise. The worked example applies this directly: three conditions, each with an owner and a date, plus one deferred record with a revisit trigger and a dated 30-day threshold review.

questions.question: The lesson gives five screens for choosing a workflow and says two of them reject a candidate outright, no matter how well it scores elsewhere. Which two?
options: Volume and variance
A measurable baseline and a named owner
Error asymmetry and volume
Variance and error asymmetry
questions.explanation: The lesson says to reject outright on the measurable baseline and the owner, because without labelled history you cannot score the agent and a workflow with no owner never ships, and it adds that no score rescues either one.

questions.question: Autonomy is decided per action rather than per agent. In the worked service desk example, what rung does an access grant above the standard role template sit at?
options: L2, because a server access change is reversible
L1, because one wrong package is expensive to unwind
L0: the agent retrieves the policy and prepares the evidence packet, and a human decides
L3, because the ticket history provides a labelled set to measure against
questions.explanation: The worked example puts the access grant above the standard template at L0, read and summarize with no write, while a human makes the decision. L1 belongs to the catalog software installation, and the labelled history is what supports the new-starter path to L2.

questions.question: What does the lesson require of the evaluation plan before the architecture is settled?
options: A held-out split, adversarial cases the history does not contain, and six metrics carrying numeric thresholds with consequences
A model judge scoring every metric before the first release
A thousand randomly sampled units labelled by the agent itself
Thresholds written qualitatively so reviewers can apply their own judgment
questions.explanation: The lesson builds the evaluation plan before the architecture: 150 units split into development and held-out sets, adversarial cases such as instructions hidden in a ticket body or a duplicate submission, and six metrics with numbers and consequences, with 'high accuracy' explicitly rejected as a threshold.

questions.question: An engineer proposes a single tool named query_sap that accepts a free-form query string, arguing it will cover every case the support team brings up in the next year. According to the lesson, why is that design rejected?
options: Because a single tool increases the token cost of the tool definitions on every turn, so the model has less room for the case context
Because the protocol requires one MCP server per system, so a single tool cannot span SAP and the warehouse at once
Because free-form tool arguments cannot be validated, which makes latency unpredictable under load
One tool that runs arbitrary queries is not least privilege, it is unbounded access with a friendly name.
questions.explanation: The lesson's tool layer rules are one tool per action and never one tool per system, and it explains the failure in those words: a broad query tool is unbounded access rather than scoped capability. The alternative it builds is a set of named tools such as get_order and get_shipment, each taking a validated identifier and returning a fixed shape.

questions.question: During the first week live, a network timeout on the return authorization call is retried by the client, and the customer receives two return labels for one case. Which design element from the lesson prevents this?
options: A per-tool timeout of three seconds with two retries and jitter applied to read tools only
The key is the case identifier plus the line item plus an action version, and the server stores the key alongside the result for 24 hours.
The iteration cap of eight tool calls per case, which bounds how often a write can be attempted
Shadow mode, which records the draft next to what the analyst actually sent so duplicates are visible
questions.explanation: The lesson states the rule that every write takes an idempotency key and that no write retries without one, and it shows the key construction and the 24 hour result store. It also notes that without this, the retry policy becomes a liability rather than a safety net.

questions.question: On a Wednesday afternoon the support lead reports that drafted return authorizations are producing wrong eligibility calls, while order status answers are fine and customers are waiting. What should the support lead reach for, per the lesson?
options: The global flag, because any quality problem justifies falling back to the pre-agent queue for all traffic
The tool flag on get_order, since the wrong eligibility call probably originates in the order data
The workflow flag is the one an on-call support lead reaches for when a single path is hurting and the rest of the traffic is fine.
The feature flag, since lowering the rollout percentage removes the affected drafts from the population
questions.explanation: The lesson separates the kill switch levels by blast radius: a tool flag for one tool, a workflow flag for one path while other traffic continues, and a global flag for all agent traffic. It also draws a line between a feature flag, which controls who sees a path, and a kill switch, which controls whether the path exists, and it requires the fallback to resume the queue in under two minutes.

questions.question: Three weeks after stage 1 opened, the human edit rate on drafted returns has risen from 12 percent to 24 percent. Complaint volume and customer satisfaction are unchanged, and nobody has rerun the golden set. What does the lesson say is happening?
options: Nothing actionable, because quality problems should be judged by customer satisfaction rather than by internal edit metrics
A rising edit rate with a flat complaint rate is a system telling you it got worse and nobody outside the team has noticed yet.
The edit rate threshold is set too low, so the fix is to raise it to 30 percent to match the regional baseline
The retrieval index has drifted, so the only reliable response is to rebuild the index from scratch
questions.explanation: The lesson names edit rate as the metric to watch in stages 1 through 3 and the one teams forget to instrument, because it moves within days of a retrieval or prompt regression, well before complaint rates move. The prescribed reading is a quality review of the top ten edits rather than a threshold adjustment, and the same signal measured against the fixed golden set of 40 cases is the comparable weekly number.

questions.question: A severity 3 quality incident on one case class is closed with six prompt edits and no new test coverage. Per the lesson, what is wrong with the closure?
options: The incident should have been escalated to severity 2, since any quality drop after launch is customer facing
Prompt edits are held in a console rather than version control, so the closure cannot be audited
Nothing, because a prompt edit is faster to apply than a code change and the incident is closed with an owner
Every postmortem produces at least one new eval case and at most one prompt change.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives the postmortem ratio directly, and it explains why the ratio matters: a team that answers every incident with a prompt edit accumulates an unreadable instruction set and no test coverage, so the same incident returns in a different disguise. At most one prompt change keeps the instruction set comprehensible, and at least one eval case converts the incident into a regression test.

questions.question: The error budget burns 40 percent of its monthly allowance in two days. A product owner argues for shipping the prompt improvement immediately, on the grounds that it will fix the problem faster than any other option. What does the lesson say the team should do?
options: Sixty cases a month is not much, and when the budget burns down the response is to stop shipping changes rather than to ship faster to fix things.
Spend the remaining budget on the fix, because an error budget exists precisely to fund corrective changes
Move the rollout back a stage for one week and then resume shipping at the same rate
Raise the availability objective to 99.9 percent so the burn no longer breaches the documented threshold
questions.explanation: The lesson treats the availability objective of 99.5 percent as a budget to spend rather than a target to hit, and states the consequence of a burn in those words. Raising an objective to escape a burn defeats the purpose, and the SRE material it cites notes that an objective which reflects what users care about should drive prioritization.

questions.question: A nightly enrichment job has processed 640 of 900 cases when its worker is terminated. The rerun finishes the remaining 260 in eleven minutes. Which design decision accounts for the cheap resume?
options: The job holds its whole run in memory and the runtime rehydrates that memory from the ledger
The retry budget was raised to five attempts per case, which absorbs a mid-run termination
Checkpoints every 100 cases mean the rerun starts at case 601 rather than case 1.
The case store enforces a unique key on the case ID, which removes the need to track progress
questions.explanation: Checkpointing writes partial state to storage during a long-running process so a later run resumes rather than starting over, which is the mechanism the lesson gives for the crash case and the reason a rerun costs one hundred cases instead of nine hundred. A unique key prevents duplicate rows but does nothing to save the recomputation, and a larger retry budget does not survive process termination on its own.

questions.question: An engineer adds a single retry to a step that appends a row to a quality table. During a slow period the step succeeds on the second attempt and the table gains two rows for the same case. Which rule did the retry break?
options: A retry is only safe when applying the change twice equals applying it once.
Retries belong on the run loop rather than on individual tool calls
A retry must be bounded by the error budget for the service before it is allowed to run
Stale data is almost always better than incorrect data, so the step should have waited
questions.explanation: The lesson states that an idempotent mutation is what makes a retry safe and that a retry on an append is a duplicate row nobody has read yet. The freshness policy is a separate pipeline decision about late input, and the run loop acts at the level of a whole execution rather than one write. Without idempotency, a retry converts a transient timeout into a data quality incident.

questions.question: A quality regression drops the golden-set pass rate below the freeze threshold for two weeks. An engineer proposes letting the loop automatically roll back the last prompt change to cut the time to recovery. What does the lesson say about that proposal?
options: It is acceptable once the rollback is dry-run against the last thirty days of cases
It is acceptable if the rollback fires a notification to the quality owner at the same time
It should be replaced by a data repair step that rewrites the affected ledger rows
Anything that changes how already-written data should be interpreted belongs to a person.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats rolling back a prompt change as a rung 5 action wearing a rung 2 costume, because it rewrites the behavior that produced two weeks of already-processed cases. Its general test is that anything changing how already-written data should be interpreted belongs to a person, and that test is offered as more durable than a fixed list of allowed actions. Notification does not change who owns the decision.
